title: Buddhism in East Asia: family, kingship, and salvation
description: From Han imperial order to Buddhist communities in China and Silla: the arguments of Mouzi, Huiyuan, and Wŏn’gwang, and their consequences for East Asia.
meta: Ebrey 56–74, 103–105 · Mouzi and Huiyuan (SCT) · Wŏn’gwang and the Silla conversion (SKT)

sections.title: What we bring from earlier classes

body.html:
Early traditions
We compared accounts of good order, ethical conduct, and rightful rule: Ru, Mo, Dao, and Fa.
Qin and Han
We then followed empire-building. Lu Jia and Dong Zhongshu made the ruler answerable to more than his own desires. October 8: Han rule.
Today’s change
Family and government remain important. Buddhism introduces a further goal: release from suffering and rebirth, pursued through lay practice and monastic life.

Course synthesis · Ebrey 20–74; SCT 416–429. The passages below show disagreements within Buddhism as well as objections to it.

sections.title: After the Han: Wei, Shu, and Wu
sections.source: Ebrey & Walthall, pp. 62–64 · China’s Three Kingdoms, not Korea’s

body.html:
▶ Open animated map · 190–280 CEPlay / pause · Year slider · Back returns to lesson

Animation: Chinese Emperor Stats · sources and method. Starts in 229; territorial zones are reconstructed from recorded city control, not exact borders.

1. 220Han ends; Wei proclaimed
  2. 263Wei defeats Shu
  3. 265Jin replaces Wei

CE · sequence, not scaled. Wu survives the replacement of Wei by Jin.

Wei · north China

Cao Cao builds northern power; his son Cao Pei / Cao Pi ends the Han. Wei is the largest of the three kingdoms.

Shu · Sichuan

Liu Bei claims Han imperial descent, supported by strategist Zhuge Liang.

Wu · the Yangzi region

The Sun Ce–Sun Quan regime controls the central and lower Yangzi and lands farther south.

Institutions outlast the rivalry: military households make soldier status hereditary; state farms provision armies; Nine Rank recruitment favors powerful families.

Political division also frames the elite culture of Wang Xizhi and the later religious communities of Huiyuan. See Ebrey’s Map 4.1, p. 63, for changing territories.

sections.title: People and events · 200–650 CE

body.p: The Han ends in 220 CE. Rival states, migration, and changing elites reshape China. Buddhism had already arrived during the Han; its later expansion depends on travel, translation, patronage, and religious appeal—not political disorder alone. Historical overview · Trade and Buddhist transmission. Overland networks connected India through Central Asia to China; monk-emissaries from Chinese states helped carry Buddhism to the Korean kingdoms. Transmission to Korea.

passage.who: Ebrey on the appeal of Buddhism
passage.quote: In a rough and tumultuous age, Buddhism offered an appealing emphasis on kindness, charity, the preservation of life, and the prospect of salvation.
passage.cite: Ebrey & Walthall, Pre-Modern East Asia, p. 70

sections.title: Wang Xizhi: handwriting and printed type
sections.source: Wang Xizhi 王羲之 · Wáng Xīzhī · fourth-century Eastern Jin · Ebrey pp. 64, 70

body.p: Another development in the same world: Wang Xizhi represents elite calligraphic culture in Eastern Jin China. The letter makes writing a personal artistic practice as well as a means of record-keeping. Calligraphy’s cultural role. His place here is a comparison within the period, not an illustration of Buddhist doctrine.

body.html:
Wang Xizhi was an Eastern Jin official and calligrapher. Timely Clearing after Snowfall survives as a Tang tracing copy; no autograph originals survive.

Wang’s letter is the large dark writing on the right-hand leaf. The small writing above and on the facing leaf is later commentary; the red marks are collectors’ seals.

The same characters in print

快雪時晴 · Kuài xuě shí qíng
“Clearing after sudden snow.”

The four outlined brush forms read downward: 1 快 → 2 雪 → 3 時 → 4 晴. Match each number to the printed character beside it.

Running script · xíngshū 行書: variable strokes and connected movement. The type beside it is modern sans-serif.

Five-minute calligraphy comparison

  1. Copy the four printed characters once.
  2. Copy their forms from the historical model.
  3. Circle differences in spacing, proportion and connections.
Whole album opening and image source

The National Palace Museum, Taipei · Object record and open-image terms · CC BY 4.0. Enlarged letter detail shown above; the full image remains intact.

Later modelbook rubbing retained as an additional reference.

sections.title: Dunhuang: Buddhism in paint, stone, and space
sections.source: Mogao Grottoes · Dunhuang, Gansu · Cave 285, 538–539 CE

body.html:
Key dates CE · sequence, not scaled

  1. 538–539Cave 285
  2. TangCave 85
  3. 868Diamond Sutra

Buddhism becomes a place

At an oasis on the Silk Road, Buddhist worship takes architectural form: caves cut into cliffs, painted walls, sculptures, and spaces for meditation.

Cave 285 belongs to the divided China on our timeline. Its paintings bring Buddhist figures together with Indian deities and Chinese mythological figures. Religious transmission produces new combinations of images as well as translated texts.

The cave’s inscriptions date it to 538–539. Its wider painted program includes Fuxi and Nüwa; the photograph at left is one detail, not the whole program.

Explore Cave 285 · Dunhuang AcademyGetty introduction · 5:31 videoContinue to Tang Dunhuang: cave and printed book

sections.title: Buddhist cave sites across Asia
Three Jewels & Four Noble Truths

body.p: Buddhism is a religious tradition originating in India, centered on the Buddha’s awakening and teachings. Siddhartha Gautama is the historical Buddha; “Buddha” means an awakened one. Lay followers support and practice the teachings; monks and nuns leave household life for a disciplined religious community. Introduction and source context · SCT 416–420.

body.html:
Three Jewels in the image

Buddha · the teacher
The seated figure at the center.
Dharma · the teaching
The wheel below his right hand: “setting the wheel of Dharma in motion.”
Sangha · the community
The five monks gathered around him.

The standing figure beside the Buddha is Vajrapani, a protector; he is not one of the monks.

Four Noble Truths

  1. Suffering — to understand.
  2. Craving, its origin — to abandon.
  3. Cessation — to realize.
  4. The Eightfold Path — to develop.

Teaching summary: SN 56.11 · The Three Refuges · SCT, pp. 416–420.

Existing Four Noble Truths infographic — Ben Lilagan, Dharma by Design

Brief reference: terms in the readings

Text outline: Three Jewels, Four Truths and Eightfold Path

Karma
Intentional action and its consequences.
Saṃsāra
The cycle of birth, death and rebirth.
Nirvana
Liberation from craving and rebirth.
Mahāyāna
“Great Vehicle”; traditions emphasizing the bodhisattva path.
Bodhisattva
A being on the path to Buddhahood; the Mahāyāna ideal joins wisdom and compassion.
No permanent self
No unchanging, independent self underlies a person’s changing parts.
Merit
Beneficial consequences of good deeds, including support for religious life.
Patronage
Material support: food, land, buildings, images or protection.

sections.title: Buddha and bodhisattva
sections.source: Two sculptures from Gandhara, in present-day Pakistan · not shown at the same scale

body.p: Mahāyāna (“Great Vehicle”) gives special importance to the bodhisattva’s pursuit of awakening for the benefit of all beings. This helps explain why Buddhist devotion includes figures such as Maitreya, not only the historical Buddha. SCT 419–420.

sections.title: Bangasayusang · Pensive Bodhisattva
sections.source: Korea · Three Kingdoms period · early 7th century

body.p: What transmission produced: Buddhist images became objects of devotion in Korea. This seventh-century sculpture, and its Japanese comparison, give material evidence for a religious culture shared across political borders.

body.html:

Pensive bodhisattvas are often associated with Maitreya, the future Buddha, called Mireuk in Korean. The museum notes a close comparison with the wooden pensive image at Kōryūji in Japan.

sections.title: Buddhism beyond the state—and in its service
sections.source: Two relationships, not two separate Buddhisms · SCT 427–429; SKT 41–48

body.html:
Key dates CE · sequence, not scaled

  1. 404Huiyuan
  2. 527Ichadon
  3. 608Wŏn’gwang

Monastic independence

Monks leave household life and join a religious community whose obligations can cross political borders.

Huiyuan: exemption from royal homage. Religious authority has a purpose the ruler cannot fulfill.

Support for royal authority

Rulers sponsor Buddhist monuments and institutions; monks can serve as royal advisers and agents.

Wŏn’gwang: service to Silla’s king. Royal obligations can conflict with a monk’s prohibition on killing.

Buddhism can limit a ruler’s claims and support royal power. Today’s readings show both.

Adapted from the class slides’ “counterculture” / state-support comparison. “Counterculture” here means an alternative community and authority—not withdrawal from all social ties.

sections.title: Mouzi: defending Buddhism with Chinese authorities
sections.source: Mouzi 牟子 · “Master Mou” · Disposing of Error, SCT pp. 421–426

body.p: The problem is belonging: shaving the head and remaining celibate challenge filial obligations. Mouzi answers with figures his opponents already respect. The defense works by interpreting Chinese tradition, not simply rejecting it.

body.html:
牟子

Mouzi · Móuzǐ

The voice of a dialogue defending Buddhism against objections about the Classics, family duties, and foreign origins. The text presents a late-Han setting; its authorship and date remain debated.

Mouzi 牟子 is not Mozi 墨子, the earlier thinker studied in this course. Text and attribution.
Filial piety · xiào 孝: duties to parents and ancestors. Leaving the household · chūjiā 出家: becoming a monk or nun changes family obligations.

pair.quote: But now the monks shave their heads. How this violates the sayings of the sages and is out of keeping with the way of the filial!
Taibo cut his hair short and tattooed his body ... And yet Confucius praised him, saying that his might well be called <mark>the ultimate virtue</mark>.
Now of felicities there is none greater than the continuation of one’s line, of unfilial conduct there is none worse than childlessness.
Boyi and Shuqi starved in Shouyang, but Confucius praised their worth. ... One does not hear of their being ill-spoken of because they were childless and propertyless.

passage.quote: The spirit never perishes. Only the body decays.
passage.cite: SCT p. 424 · compare the editors on p. 416: no eternal Self or soul

body.html:
Names in Mouzi’s replies

Taibo
Yields succession and adopts Wu customs; Mouzi cites Confucius’s praise despite his cut hair and tattoos. Analects 8.1.
Boyi and Shuqi
Brothers remembered for refusing Zhou service and starving at Shouyang. Shiji 61 · Chinese primary text.
Bian Que
A celebrated physician; Mouzi uses medicine to defend drawing on different sources. Shiji 105 · Chinese primary text.

sections.title: Gentlemen and “barbarian” practices: PRO / CON
sections.source: Mouzi’s debate · earlier precedent: the king of Zhao’s foreign dress

body.html:
Living among foreigners

PRO

Mouzi cites Confucius

“If a noble person dwells in their midst, what rudeness can there be among them?”

SCT p. 425; Analects 9.14, quoted by Mouzi. October 13 reader

CON

The questioner cites Confucius

“The barbarians with a ruler are not so good as the Chinese without one.”

SCT p. 425; Analects 3.5, quoted by the questioner. October 13 reader

Passage context and translation note

Mouzi invokes Confucius’s proposed residence among the “nine barbarian nations.” This supports living among outsiders; it does not itself say that all customs are equally good. The CON quotation follows the assigned translation of a disputed Analects passage.

Learning from foreign teachings

PRO

Mouzi

“What accords with rightness is to be followed, what heals the sick is good. The gentleman-scholar draws widely on all forms of good and thereby benefits his character.”

SCT pp. 421–422. October 13 reader

CON

The questioner cites Mencius

“I have heard of using what is Chinese to change what is barbarian, but I have never heard of using what is barbarian to change what is Chinese.”

SCT p. 425; Mengzi 3A4, quoted by the questioner. October 13 reader

Adopting foreign dress

PRO

The king of Zhao

“Clothes exist to be useful and manners respond to conditions.”

“The King of Zhao Convinces His Uncle to Wear Barbarian Dress,” Ebrey & Walthall, p. 25; trans. J. I. Crump, modified.

CON

Gongzi Cheng, the king’s uncle

“But now the king would discard all this and wear the habit of foreign regions.”

Same passage, Ebrey & Walthall, p. 25.

Passage context

The king connects Hu dress with mounted archery and border defense. His uncle initially treats the change as abandoning inherited civilization, then accepts the king’s argument.

Scope of this comparison

PRO: reasons to engage with foreign people, teachings, or practices. CON: reasons to resist. The sources address different actions: living among foreigners, learning from them, and adopting their dress.

sections.title: Huiyuan: monks and royal authority
sections.source: Huiyuan, A Monk Does Not Bow Down Before a King · SCT pp. 427–429

body.html:
Key dates CE · sequence, not scaled

  1. 334–416Huiyuan’s life
  2. 404Essay on royal homage

body.p: The institutional consequence: a monastery is a community with obligations distinct from the household. Huiyuan defends monks’ exemption from royal homage while affirming lay followers’ duties to parents and rulers. This is a claim about religious and ritual status, not modern separation of religion and state.

body.html:
Huiyuan 慧遠 · Huìyuǎn

334–416 · Mount Lu, southern China

A monk and community leader at Donglin Temple. His A Monk Does Not Bow Down Before a King dates to 404, during the controversy over Huan Xuan’s demand for monastic obeisance.

His distinction: householders follow ordinary family and political duties; monastics serve a religious purpose that warrants a different ritual status.

Biographical background · SCT pp. 427–429.

pair.who: Those who stay in the household
pair.quote: Therefore they who rejoice in the way of Śākya invariably first serve their parents and respect their lords.

Kings and princes, though they have the power of preserving existence, <mark>cannot cause a preserved creature to be without woe</mark>. ... This is why the monk refuses homage to the Lord of the Myriad Chariots

sections.title: Korea’s Three Kingdoms: rival states, shared connections
sections.source: Ebrey & Walthall, pp. 103–105 · stop before “Unification by Silla”

body.html:
Goguryeo · Koguryŏ

Northern peninsula and southern Manchuria. A military power connected to Inner Asian conflicts; expansion southward puts pressure on its neighbors.

Baekje · Paekche

Southwest. A maritime kingdom with Chinese and Japanese connections. Official ranks and local administration strengthen royal control.

Silla

Southeast. Tribal leadership develops into a stronger monarchy, with a law code, taxation, a war ministry, and state-sponsored Buddhism.

Also on the map: Gaya

A southern confederation known for iron and trade with Japan. Silla absorbs its last remaining territory in 562.

Ebrey’s political context: warfare, administrative borrowing, and control of labor help kings build states. Tombs and fortresses make elite power visible.

Ichadon and royal patronage belong inside this process. Wŏn’gwang’s petition addresses conflict between these kingdoms.

sections.title: Silla: conversion and royal patronage

body.html:
Key dates CE · sequence, not scaled

  1. 527Ichadon’s martyrdom
  2. 608Petition to Sui
  3. 1215Kakhun’s account

body.p: A different political setting: Silla is one of three competing Korean kingdoms. In this conversion narrative, Pŏphŭng seeks royal support for Buddhism while ministers resist. Ich’adon’s death legitimizes the king’s religious policy within the story. Ebrey 103–105; SKT 41–44.

body.html:
527 · the conversion narrative’s date

The ministers object

“In recent years the crops have been scarce, and the people are restless. Besides, because of frequent border raids from the neighboring state, our soldiers are still engaged in battle.”

SKT pp. 41–42. Oct 13 reader · p. 6

Ich’adon

“Sacrificing his life in order to accomplish goodness is the great principle of the official.”

SKT p. 42. Oct 13 reader · p. 6

Gyeongju National Museum: the later monument and martyrdom narrative.

People and the later written source

Pŏphŭng · Beopheung

The king associated with Silla’s official acceptance of Buddhism. The reading calls him Pŏpkong, his monastic name.

Ich’adon

The court official whose execution and miraculous death mark the conversion account, dated 527.

A later sacred biography

The account survives in Kakhun’s Lives of Eminent Korean Monks (1215). Miracles are the narrative’s claims.

sections.title: Wŏn’gwang and the petition for troops
sections.source: Wŏn’gwang 圓光 · Wongwang in modern romanization · Silla monk and royal adviser

body.html:
걸사표 乞師表

Geolsapyo · Petition Requesting Troops

Requested by: King Chinp’yŏng of Silla.
Addressed to: the Sui court.
Purpose: military help against Koguryŏ.

The petition’s original wording does not survive. The passage below records the monk’s reply to his king, not the text sent to Sui.

  1. 608The king commissions Wŏn’gwang to draft it.
  2. 611Silla’s embassy requests troops, according to the historical account.
  3. 612Sui launches its major invasion of Koguryŏ. Do not reduce the war’s causes to this petition.

Academy of Korean Studies: petition, dates, and lost text · Samguk sagi: the 608 entry.

body.p: Read Wŏn’gwang’s reply and lay commandments beside Laozi below ↓

body.html:
Names and institutions in the rest of the Silla reading
Chajang · Jajang 자장
A monk who studied in Tang China and became Silla’s national monastic overseer. SKT pp. 46–48.
Hwarang 화랑 · “flower youths”
Silla youth groups associated with elite cultivation, royal recruitment, and military service. SKT pp. 54–55.
Kwanch’ang · Gwanchang 관창
The young hwarang whose death in battle becomes an example of loyalty and courage. SKT pp. 55–56.
Chin’gol · jingol 진골 · “true bone”
A hereditary elite rank in Silla’s status hierarchy. Chajang’s biography names this background.

sections.title: Laozi and Wŏn’gwang: killing in war
sections.source: Laozi, chapter 31 · Wŏn’gwang’s reply and Five Commandments for Laymen

body.html: Using force under constraint

pair.quote: Weapons are inauspicious instruments, not the instruments of a cultivated person. But if given no other choice, the cultivated person will use them.
pair.cite: Laozi 31, trans. Philip J. Ivanhoe, Readings in Classical Chinese Philosophy, 3rd ed., p. 187

pair.who: Wŏn’gwang’s reported reply to the king
pair.quote: To destroy others in order to preserve oneself is not the way of a monk. But since I, a poor monk, live in Your Majesty’s territory and waste Your Majesty’s clothes and food, I dare not disobey.

body.p: Laozi allows the use of weapons when there is no other choice. Wŏn’gwang says destruction violates a monk’s way, but agrees to serve the king who sustains him.

body.html: Victory, mourning, and battlefield duty

pair.quote: A military victory is not a thing of beauty. To beautify victory is to delight in the slaughter of human beings. ... When great numbers of people have been killed, one weeps for them in grief and sorrow. <mark>Military victory is associated with the rites of mourning.</mark>
pair.cite: Laozi 31, trans. Philip J. Ivanhoe, p. 187

pair.quote: serve your sovereign with loyalty; attend your parents with filial piety; treat your friends with sincerity; <mark>do not retreat from a battlefield</mark>; be discriminating about the taking of life.

body.p: Even victory does not justify delight in killing. Laozi prescribes grief and mourning. Wŏn’gwang’s lay precepts combine battlefield loyalty with restraint in taking life; they do not prescribe withdrawal from war.

body.html: The first Laozi excerpt restores lines from the full assigned source that the compact reading omitted. The English quotations above retain Ivanhoe’s translation.

sections.title: Seasonal killing rules before Buddhism in China
sections.source: Earlier Chinese parallels · Wŏn’gwang’s rules for laypeople

body.p: Seasonal restrictions on killing already appear in Warring States Chinese texts. They precede Buddhism’s establishment in China. Wŏn’gwang’s rule combines a spring–summer restriction with Buddhist fasting days.

pair.who: Earlier Chinese ritual rule · First month of spring
pair.quote: Nests should not be thrown down; unformed insects should not be killed, nor creatures in the Womb, nor very young creatures
pair.cite: Liji (Book of Rites), “Yue Ling” (Monthly Ordinances), §10; trans. James Legge

pair.quote: Not to kill during the months of <mark>spring and summer</mark> nor during the six meatless feast days is to choose the time.

body.html:
Xunzi · 3rd century BCE

Wangzhi (“The Regulations of a King”), chapter 9, bars nets and poisons from marshes while aquatic animals breed. It explicitly protects their growth and links seasonal restraint to plentiful resources.

Primary text · §22 · summary, not a quotation.

Lüshi chunqiu · c. 239 BCE

The first spring month’s ordinances prohibit destroying nests and killing unborn or young creatures. Fawns and eggs are protected too. Closely parallel wording appears in the Liji.

Text and parallel passages · Compilation date. Summary.

Wŏn’gwang · Early 7th century CE

The reported teaching adds six Buddhist observance days to the seasonal rule. It also selects which creatures may be killed and discourages killing often.

SKT p. 46 · Samguk yusa translation, pp. 473–474, note 22. Summary.

body.p: The distinction: earlier Chinese rules protect reproduction and regulate taking animal life by season; Buddhist precepts supply a broader objection to killing. The resemblance is clear. Direct borrowing by Wŏn’gwang from a particular Chinese text is not established by these passages.

body.html: “Birthing season” is an explanation of the seasonal logic, not Wŏn’gwang’s wording in the assigned translation. His text says “spring and summer.” The account is preserved in later compilations, not a surviving contemporary transcript.

sections.title: From restrictions on killing to vegetarian practice

body.html:
A rule against killing does not always mean a rule against eating meat. Chinese Buddhist vegetarianism developed through debates about compassion, monastic discipline, and the authority to set religious rules.

Earlier Chinese restraint
Meat abstinence could express mourning or ritual discipline. Seasonal rules protected animals at particular times. Neither practice necessarily required lifelong vegetarianism. Historical study · earlier Chinese passages.
Early Buddhist permission
The Jīvaka Sutta, MN 55, permits meat when the recipient has not seen, heard, or suspected that the animal was killed specifically for them. Responsibility for killing matters; meat is not categorically forbidden.
A stronger Mahāyāna prohibition
The Fanwang Sutra, third minor precept, p. 47, prohibits eating meat and connects the prohibition to compassion. This is a supplement to the major precept against killing in our assigned excerpt—not the same passage.
Emperor Wu of Liang · r. 502–549
Emperor Wu pressed monks to abandon meat, helping institutionalize vegetarianism in Chinese Buddhism. He did not invent abstinence or make the whole population vegetarian.

Compare the scope: seasonal restraint limits when killing occurs; the early Buddhist permission concerns who caused the killing; the Fanwang Sutra restricts eating meat itself. Wŏn’gwang’s rules for laypeople combine loyalty and selective restraint. These positions overlap; they are not stages that every Buddhist community passed through.

Course synthesis; source links above. The Liang debates belong to the early sixth century. Their exact dating is disputed, so no single year is assigned here. Emperor Wu adds another contrast with Huiyuan: a ruler attempts to determine monastic conduct.

sections.title: Looking ahead: painted caves and printed scriptures

body.html:
The sixth-century cave is part of Tuesday’s world. These later works show what sustained Buddhist patronage and the circulation of texts will produce under the Tang.

The larger story: Buddhism connects patrons, artisans, monasteries, and readers. A religious teaching becomes a lasting part of East Asia’s material and intellectual culture.

sections.title: What changes in East Asian history

body.html: <dl class="course-connections"><dt>Family and community</dt><dd>Monastic life organizes a community outside marriage and descent. That makes celibacy, filial duty, and support for religious communities matters of public debate.</dd><dt>Political authority</dt><dd>Rulers gain religious allies, advisers, and institutions to sponsor. Huiyuan defends exemption from royal homage; Wŏn’gwang accepts royal service despite its conflict with monastic commitments.</dd><dt>A connected East Asia</dt><dd>Texts, monks, images, and practices move across borders. Local patrons and courts reshape them. Shared religion does not erase different kingdoms or competing interests.</dd></dl>

passage.quote: in China the governments successfully claimed the authority to regulate Buddhist clergy and monastic establishments.
passage.cite: Ebrey & Walthall, Pre-Modern East Asia, p. 72

body.html:
Next: Sui–Tang models, Korea, and Japan · October 15

Imperial reunification will operate in a world already transformed by Buddhist institutions. Chajang’s work in Silla—monastic regulation and court adoption of Chinese practices—connects today’s readings to the next class on adapting continental models. SKT 46–48; October 15 reader.

For the Great Debate · October 20

The Fo position must explain what religious practice contributes to the realm and what it may refuse the ruler. Mouzi, Huiyuan, and Wŏn’gwang supply different arguments—not one unanimous Buddhist policy. Great Debate guide.

overview:
Dunhuang · explore the cave paintings 538–539 → Tang → 868

Buddhism offers liberation from suffering and rebirth, and a community organized around that goal. In China and Korea, it creates new claims on people’s loyalties, labor, and wealth—alongside those of family and ruler.

Three voices in the readings

Mouzi
Defends a foreign teaching through Chinese precedents. The dialogue’s date and authorship are debated.
Huiyuan · 334–416
Defends a distinct status for monks: a ruler can sustain life but cannot end suffering.
Wŏn’gwang · early 7th century
Accepts obligations to Silla’s king, even when royal service conflicts with a monk’s prohibition on killing.
